## Where do ERGM parameter values come from?

This short walkthrough gives some intuition behind the coefficient values that are estimated when you run an ERGM.

## Load some libraries

Let's first load our libraries.

```{r}
library(statnet)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Create simulated data

Now, let's suppose we go out in the world and collect some network data. Ultimately we want to model the data to get a better sense of the processes that may be at work in determining the ties. Rather than actually collecting data, let's play god for a minute and simulate some data. The benefit of this, for our purposes, is that we know the true data generating process, and so we know the true coefficient values that generated our observed data. We will call this network `g.true`.



```{r}
set.seed(181318)
# simulate() needs enough steps (the burn-in) to get from its starting network
# to a typical network from the model. The default (16,384 steps) is too short
# here, so the simulated networks would have too few ties. We use 100,000 steps
# for this and every simulation below.
ctrl <- control.simulate.formula(MCMC.burnin = 100000)

# network.initialize(57) creates an empty directed network with 57 nodes.
# simulate() uses it only as a starting point: it adds and removes ties one
# at a time, following the model (edges = -1, mutual = 2), until the network
# is a typical draw from that model. The empty start doesn't affect the result.
g.true <- simulate(network.initialize(57) ~ edges + mutual, coef = c(-1, 2), nsim = 1,
                   control = ctrl)
summary(g.true ~ edges + mutual)
```

Based on the data we created, the observed number of edges is `r summary(g.true ~ edges)` and there are `r summary(g.true ~ mutual)` mutual ties. Let's save these values and plot the data.


```{r}
true.edges = summary(g.true ~ edges)
true.mutual = summary(g.true ~ mutual)
plot(g.true)
```

## Identify the true parameter values

Now we will assume we don't know the coefficient values used to simulate the data. We will therefore proceed by simulating a bunch of networks with different values to try to home in on the correct coefficients. This may have you asking: how do we know we have obtained the "correct" coefficients? If you have taken a course on maximum likelihood, you know that, in a nutshell, you are searching for the parameter values that make the data you observed the most probable, given your model. We will do the same thing here with our network data.

As we saw above, we know the variables that generated our data, and hopefully our theory correctly guided us to include them in our model. With ERGMs, we are attempting to reproduce a set of target statistics. Given our model with an edges term and a mutual term, we would like our model to produce data (i.e., simulate data) that make our observed statistics on these terms the most probable.

OK, let's see this in action. Let's assume we don't know the true model that generated the `g.true` network. So we don't know the coefficients, but we have the observed data, and we know how many edges and mutual ties there are in our data.

Again, let's also assume we have some theory which (correctly) tells us that the two key processes that built up our data can be captured by the following ERGM terms: edges and mutual. Thus, our nodes have some underlying tendency to form ties (this is our edges term) and also a tendency to form mutual ties.

So now we need to explore possible values for our coefficients. Obviously, there are algorithms operating under the hood of the `ergm()` function that do this much more efficiently, but to give you some intuition, we will just try out some values until we find what look like good estimates.

### Try 1: edges = −2, mutual = .5

Let's try −2 and .5. Given those values, we will simulate 200 different networks that could be produced by those coefficients.

```{r}
g.sim <- simulate(network.initialize(57) ~ edges + mutual, coef = c(-2, .5),
                  nsim = 200, sequential = FALSE, control = ctrl)
```

Note: sequential = FALSE starts each of the 200 simulations from the same initial network, so the 200 networks are independent draws from the model.

And just out of curiosity, we can take a look at the summary statistics for the first simulated network.

```{r}
summary(g.sim[[1]] ~ edges + mutual)
```

Here, we can see we are way off the true values. We are only producing `r summary(g.sim[[1]] ~ edges)` edges and only `r summary(g.sim[[1]] ~ mutual)` mutuals. And while this is only one of our simulated networks, we suspect that these are likely not the correct coefficients, as they are unlikely to have created our true network. To provide more insight into this and use all of our simulated data, let's grab the count of edges and mutuals for all simulated networks and plot that distribution against the values we found in our true network. I'll plot the true values in blue.

```{r}
g.sim.edges = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.edges[i] = summary(g.sim[[i]] ~ edges)

g.sim.mutual = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.mutual[i] = summary(g.sim[[i]] ~ mutual)

g.sim.data = as.data.frame(cbind(g.sim.edges, g.sim.mutual))

ggplot(g.sim.data, aes(x = g.sim.edges, y = g.sim.mutual)) + geom_point() +
  annotate("point", x = true.edges, y = true.mutual, colour = "blue", size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Edges", y = "Mutual ties", title = "edges = -2, mutual = .5") # added: axis labels

colMeans(g.sim.data) # added: the average simulated statistics
```

Note, the additional `geom_point()` plots the location of our observed data, which had `r true.edges` edges and `r true.mutual` mutual ties.

When we plot the number of edges versus mutual ties for all of the networks simulated from this model, we see that our observed data is nowhere near that distribution: the simulated networks average `r round(mean(g.sim.edges))` edges and `r round(mean(g.sim.mutual))` mutual ties. It is unlikely we would ever observe our data if these were in fact the correct parameters.

### Try 2: edges = −1.5, mutual = .75

So what happens now is that we need to update our parameters. Because we underestimated the number of edges and mutuals, let's increase these values and repeat the process.

```{r}
g.sim2 <- simulate(network.initialize(57) ~ edges + mutual, coef = c(-1.5, .75),
                   nsim = 200, sequential = FALSE, control = ctrl)

g.sim.edges = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.edges[i] = summary(g.sim2[[i]] ~ edges)

g.sim.mutual = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.mutual[i] = summary(g.sim2[[i]] ~ mutual)

g.sim.data = as.data.frame(cbind(g.sim.edges, g.sim.mutual))

ggplot(g.sim.data, aes(x = g.sim.edges, y = g.sim.mutual)) + geom_point() +
  annotate("point", x = true.edges, y = true.mutual, colour = "blue", size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Edges", y = "Mutual ties", title = "edges = -1.5, mutual = .75")

colMeans(g.sim.data)
```

Still not great (an average of `r round(mean(g.sim.edges))` edges and `r round(mean(g.sim.mutual))` mutual ties). Let's increase our parameter values again.

### Try 3: edges = −1, mutual = 1

```{r}
g.sim3 <- simulate(network.initialize(57) ~ edges + mutual, coef = c(-1, 1),
                   nsim = 200, sequential = FALSE, control = ctrl)

g.sim.edges = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.edges[i] = summary(g.sim3[[i]] ~ edges)

g.sim.mutual = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.mutual[i] = summary(g.sim3[[i]] ~ mutual)

g.sim.data = as.data.frame(cbind(g.sim.edges, g.sim.mutual))

ggplot(g.sim.data, aes(x = g.sim.edges, y = g.sim.mutual)) + geom_point() +
  annotate("point", x = true.edges, y = true.mutual, colour = "blue", size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Edges", y = "Mutual ties", title = "edges = -1, mutual = 1")

colMeans(g.sim.data)
```

This is better (an average of `r round(mean(g.sim.edges))` edges and `r round(mean(g.sim.mutual))` mutual ties), but still short. Let's try to improve.

### Try 4: edges = −.5, mutual = 2

```{r}
g.sim4 <- simulate(network.initialize(57) ~ edges + mutual, coef = c(-.5, 2),
                   nsim = 200, sequential = FALSE, control = ctrl)

g.sim.edges = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.edges[i] = summary(g.sim4[[i]] ~ edges)

g.sim.mutual = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.mutual[i] = summary(g.sim4[[i]] ~ mutual)

g.sim.data = as.data.frame(cbind(g.sim.edges, g.sim.mutual))

ggplot(g.sim.data, aes(x = g.sim.edges, y = g.sim.mutual)) + geom_point() +
 annotate("point", x = true.edges, y = true.mutual, colour = "blue", size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Edges", y = "Mutual ties", title = "edges = -.5, mutual = 2")

colMeans(g.sim.data)
```

Now we overshot the observed number of edges and mutuals (an average of `r round(mean(g.sim.edges))` edges and `r round(mean(g.sim.mutual))` mutual ties). Let's decrease the edges coefficient.

### Try 5: edges = −1, mutual = 2

```{r}
g.sim5 <- simulate(network.initialize(57) ~ edges + mutual, coef = c(-1, 2),
                   nsim = 200, sequential = FALSE, control = ctrl)
summary(g.sim5[[15]] ~ edges + mutual)

g.sim.edges = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.edges[i] = summary(g.sim5[[i]] ~ edges)

g.sim.mutual = vector()
for (i in 1:200)
  g.sim.mutual[i] = summary(g.sim5[[i]] ~ mutual)

g.sim.data = as.data.frame(cbind(g.sim.edges, g.sim.mutual))

ggplot(g.sim.data, aes(x = g.sim.edges, y = g.sim.mutual)) + geom_point() +
 annotate("point", x = true.edges, y = true.mutual, colour = "blue", size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Edges", y = "Mutual ties", title = "edges = -1, mutual = 2")

colMeans(g.sim.data)
```

So we can see that when we get the coefficients right, in this case those that match the true data generating process, we simulate networks that make our observed network central in the distribution of simulated networks. The simulated networks average `r round(mean(g.sim.edges))` edges and `r round(mean(g.sim.mutual))` mutual ties, compared with the observed `r true.edges` and `r true.mutual`.

## Letting ergm do the search

Now let's have `ergm()` do the search for us.

```{r}
fit <- ergm(g.true ~ edges + mutual, control = control.ergm(seed = 181318))
summary(fit)
```

The estimates are close to the true values of −1 and 2, but not identical. That is expected. The true coefficients make networks *like* ours central on average, but our observed network is just one draw from that model. The maximum likelihood estimates are the values that put *this particular* network at the center of the simulated distribution. The standard errors tell us how far the estimates could plausibly be from the true values given that randomness.


## Summary

To summarize Koskinen and Snijders (2013): what we are doing to solve the likelihood equation is choosing a value of θ, simulating graphs x~1~, x~2~, …, x~m~, calculating from that sample of graphs the mean of the statistics of interest (here, edges and mutual), and then checking whether the estimated mean from the simulated graphs is equal to the observed value of those statistics. If the difference is not zero, we choose another value of θ and repeat the process. This is done until we find a value for which the estimated mean of our statistics from the simulated graphs equals our observed values for those statistics. This is the MLE.

Formally, the MLE is the value of θ that solves

$$E_{\theta}\left[z(X)\right] = z(x_{\text{obs}})$$

where z(·) is the vector of model statistics (here, the counts of edges and mutual ties), x~obs~ is the observed network, and the left side is the expected value of those statistics: their average across all the networks the model with coefficients θ could produce. We can't list all those networks, so in practice we estimate that average from networks simulated from the model, as we did above. In plain terms: find the coefficients under which the model's networks have, on average, the same statistics as the observed network.

Note, a brute force approach such as the one attempted above is not very efficient. Statnet has built-in algorithms that make the search process much more efficient. But the idea is the same.
